title: attention-hotpath-hypothesis-log
content:
Purpose:
This is a lightweight running log of hypotheses, quick microbench experiments, and actionable next steps for attention hotpath behavior we observed in the field. Focus: flash-style kernels vs paged attention vs fused ops when running typical production workloads (continuous batching + long contexts). Aim is to capture reproducible checks and a short ledger of what to try next.

Context / problem statement:
- Multiple customer incidents and internal canary runs have surfaced intermittent latency regressions and high tail for models using FlashAttention-optimized kernels.
- Symptoms: single-request p95 spikes at high seq lengths (>1024), throughput drop when concurrent batch size grows beyond 4, and occasional microstutter (~50–200ms) even when average latency looks fine.
- Hypothesis space: kernel launch overheads, increased kernel count for paged flows, memory bandwidth saturation for fused ops, serialization on CPU-side scheduling, and stream/contention for async memcpy.

Quick summary of what we tried (high level):
- Microbench harness (see commands below) to measure: kernel_count, per-kernel time, memcpy time, CPU-side scheduling time (host->device enqueue), and occupancy estimates from nsys traces.
- Compared three modes: FLASH (FlashAttention kernel path), PAGED (paged KV/cache-backed attention), FUSED (operator-fusion variants that combine matmul+softmax+apply).
- Observed: FLASH wins for single-shot long contexts (seq 2k) on latency but regresses in contended scenarios; PAGED reduces memory footprint and avoids OOM at long contexts but has 10–25% higher total kernel time due to many small kernels; FUSED showed modest steady speedup in isolated runs but introduced CPU jitter when combined with continuous batching pipeline.

Representative microbench commands (harness in repo: tools/attn_microbench):
- python tools/attn_microbench/run.py --model llm-7b --kernel flash --seq 2048 --batch 1 --warmup 10 --iter 50 --profile nsys --out out/flash_seq2048.json
- python tools/attn_microbench/run.py --model llm-7b --kernel paged --seq 2048 --batch 1 --warmup 10 --iter 50 --profile nsys --out out/paged_seq2048.json
- python tools/attn_microbench/run.py --model llm-7b --kernel fused --seq 1024 --batch 4 --warmup 20 --iter 200 --concurrent 8 --out out/fused_concurrent.json
- nsys stats out/*.qdrep --section 'CUDA Kernel' --trace-summary > nsys_kernel_summary.txt

Key findings (numbers are median across 5 runs unless noted):
- Single-shot long context (seq=2048, batch=1): FLASH median token-generate = 72ms/token; PAGED = 110ms/token; FUSED = 65ms/token. Flash is good here but only when not contending.
- Concurrent small batches (seq=512, batch=4, concurrent=8): FLASH p95 increased by ~1.9x compared to baseline; PAGED p95 increased by ~1.3x; FUSED p95 increased by ~2.3x but mean was slightly better.
- Kernel counts per forward (approx): FLASH: 6 kernels, PAGED: 18 kernels, FUSED: 4 kernels. More kernels => more launch overhead and scheduling pressure.
- memcpy behavior: with default pinned-mem disabled, host->device memcpy accounted for 12–18% of wall time in concurrent runs. Enabling pinned memory reduced memcpy wall time by ~40% in experiments.
- Occupancy: nsight samples show FLASH sometimes leaves SM occupancy suboptimal at smaller batch sizes because of large register/shared usage per thread-block; paged kernels have better occupancy scaling at lower sequence lengths.

Hypotheses (ranked by how quickly we can test them):
1) Kernel launch overheads matter for small per-layer work: when continuous batching increases concurrent kernel launches, paged flow wins because it amortizes work differently. Quick test: coalesce kernels in the opchain or increase per-kernel work via batching within kernel.
2) Fused ops reduce global device-side BLAS calls but shift more work to custom kernels that may increase register pressure and reduce occupancy, causing jitter under concurrency. Test: build a low-reg-set variant of fused kernel (reduce autotune choices) and compare.
3) CPU-side scheduling bottleneck: our executor enqueues many small kernels from multiple threads; lock contention or stream contention creates tails. Test: instrument our enqueue path, try single-producer thread + batched enqueue to a single stream.
4) Async memcpy/streams misconfiguration: some codepaths use default stream vs dedicated streams causing implicit syncs. Test: force dedicated streams + explicit memcpyAsync + cudaEvent sync and rerun.
5) KV cache fragmentation in paged mode increases page-table churn on GPU causing occasional page faults (observed on device logs). Test: run with bigger page chunk size and see memory allocator behavior.

Repro checklist (short):
- Reproduce locally on our 80GB A100 node (nv-driver 525.x) and on customer-reported infra (A10x in cloud).
- Run microbench with --profile nsys and collect qdrep and summary.
- Capture per-kernel timings and kernel names; compute launch_count and average_launch_time.
- Run with pinned mem toggled and record memcpy % time.
- Run with single-stream serialized enqueue vs many-streams.

Immediate experiments to run (assigned):
- Priya: add detailed enqueue traces (timing of enqueue syscall + lock wait) to runtime for 1 week. JIRA INF-3421 assigned to Priya.
- Liu: prototype a 'batched-kernel-launch' wrapper in opchain that groups small kernels across heads and layers. Measure median/p95. Due EOW.
- Marta: reproduce the memcpy/pinned effect on A10x and produce step-by-step repro notes.

Longer-term ideas / engineering tradeoffs:
- Build a hybrid scheduler that picks kernel grouping strategy based on current concurrency and batched queue length. This trades increased code complexity for potential tail reduction.
- Expose an ops-level flag to prefer fewer kernels (aggressive fusion) vs better occupancy (less fusion) per model profile.
- Add a runtime telemetry tag that surfaces kernel_count per request in the Console so customers can correlate spikes with opchain variants.

Quick notes / gotchas seen while iterating:
- Some PyTorch fused kernels are highly sensitive to minor changes in input shapes; results not stable across PyTorch minor versions. Pinning runtime in our CI for kernels is important.
- When running nsight on multi-tenant nodes, traces can be polluted; use isolated node or minimal background processes.
- A few customer incidents were tied to driver/kernel combos (CUDA 12 vs 11.x behaviour differences). Always record driver version in ticket.

Next steps (concrete):
- Run the 'enqueue trace' build in canary (5% traffic) for 48h and collect tail metrics. (owner: Priya)
- Merge quick opt: enable pinned mem by default for serving-runtime when device mem > 32GB (owner: Marta)
- Prototype opchain batched-launch and run perf experiment across seqs=[512,1024,2048] and concurrents=[1,4,8]. (owner: Liu)
- Draft a short playbook summarizing when to pick FLASH vs PAGED vs FUSED for customers; include recommended flags. (owner: Daniel)

Logs / raw outputs (where to find):
- out/bench_runs/flash_seq2048_* under CI runner 3 (s3://redwood-perf/attn/2024-11)
- nsys_trace qdrep files under nsys/ folder in artifacts
- enqueue trace logs: /var/log/redwood/attn_enqueue.log (rotating)

Open questions (for next sync):
- What is an acceptable p95 vs median tradeoff for our SLAs when choosing kernel default? (product alignment needed)
- Should Dedicated customers get a different default kernel schedule (e.g., default to fused for low-latency single-tenant)?

Notes-to-self / rough TODOs (short):
- Add small script to parse qdrep into CSV of kernel_name,kernel_time,launch_count
- Compare results vs upstream FlashAttention v2 and list differences
- File PR to make pinned-mem setting configurable via runtime config

References and related:
- flashattention upstream repo: https://github.com/flash-attention/flash-attention
- internal PR comparing kernels: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/487
- JIRA issue tracking: INF-3421 (enqueue tracing & pinned mem experiments)

End of log (running ledger)
